source_text: δὲ, γέγονας παραβάτης νόμου.» Πεπλημμεληκότι γὰρ ἅπαξ, ἤγουν ὅτι παρανενόμηκεν ὅλως, κἂν γοῦν ἐφ' ἑνὶ καὶ ἐκ μέρους, ἕψεταί που πάντως αὐτῷ τὸ ἐγκαλεῖσθαι δεῖν. Μιαρὸς οὖν ἄρα κατὰ τὸν νόμον, κἂν εἰ μή τις ἴοι πρὸς ἔσχατον μολυσμοῦ, καταφωρῷτο δὲ πεπονθὼς κἂν γοῦν ἐκ μέρους αὐτόν. Πλὴν, οὐκ ἀπόβλητος παντελῶς, καθαίρεται δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς δι' ὕδατος ἐν Χριστῷ. Τοιγάρτοι τῆς ἐπιδημίας καιρὸν, ὑπεμφήνειεν ἂν εὖ μάλα, τὸ μέχρις ἑσπέρας ἀκάθαρτον εἶναι λέγειν τὸν μεμολυσμένον. Ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ γὰρ, μόνον δὲ οὐχὶ καὶ ἐπ' αὐταῖς ἥκοντος ἤδη δυσμαῖς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, παραγέγονεν ὁ Χριστὸς, δι' οὗ καὶ ἐν ᾧ πάντα μὲν ῥύπον ἐκνενίμμεθα τὸν ἐξ ἁμαρτίας, ἀπηλλάγμεθα δὲ μικρῶν καὶ μεγάλων αἰτιαμάτων οἱ ταῖς πλημμελείαις ἐνισχημένοι. Ὅτι δὲ πρὸ τῶν τῆς ἐπιδημίας καιρῶν οὐκ ἦν ἀπονίψασθαι μολυσμὸν (ἐδικαιοῦτο γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐν νόμῳ, κατὰ τὰς Γραφὰς), ἀναμάθοις ἂν διὰ τοῦ φάναι σαφῶς, ὅτι «Ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται ἕως ἑσπέρας.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Συνίημι ὃ φὴς, καὶ ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος. {ΚΥΡ.} Προσεπάγει δὲ τούτοις ὁ νόμος τὰ περὶ γυναικὸς, τῆς ῥεούσης αἵματι, καὶ ἀσχέτῳ καταφορᾷ τὸ καταμιαίνεσθαι δεῖν νοσούσης ἐφ' ἑαυτῇ· καὶ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ γονοῤῥυοῦς πᾶν σκεῦος κατεμολύνετο, καὶ κοίτη πᾶσα, καὶ πᾶν ἱμάτιον, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἁπτόμενος ἀγχοῦ τε ἰών· οὕτω καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῆς. Ἀπαλλάττει δὲ καὶ αὐτὴν κατὰ τὸν ἴσον ἐκείνῳ τρόπον, ὕδατι διανίζων, καὶ τρυγόνων καταθυομένων, καὶ μέντοι καὶ ἱλασμοῦ τοῦ μεσιτεύοντος ἱερέως. Ἀνακομίζων δὲ ὥσπερ εἰς ἐννοίας ἡμᾶς τὰς πνευματικὰς ὁ νόμος, καὶ τοῖς τῆς σαρκὸς ἀῤῥωστήμασιν ἐμφιλοχωρεῖν οὐκ ἐῶν (παρελήφθη γὰρ εἰς τύπον τῶν εἰς νοῦν ἔσω καὶ νοητῶν), ἐπάγει σαφῶς· «Καὶ εὐλαβεῖς ποιήσετε τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκαθαρσιῶν αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐκ ἀποθανοῦνται διὰ τὴν ἀκαθαρσίαν αὐτῶν, ἐν τῷ μιαίνειν αὐτοὺς τὴν σκηνήν μου τὴν ἐν αὐτοῖς·» κεκαθαρμένοι γὰρ δὴ καὶ ἡγιασμένοι διὰ Χριστοῦ, τότε δὴ, τότε λαμπροὶ προσίεμεν ἀληθῶς, καὶ οὐ μιανοῦμεν ἔτι τὴν ἁγίαν σκηνήν· προσκυνήσομεν δὲ καθαροὶ καθαρῶς τῷ παναγίῳ Θεῶ φοιτῶντες ἐν ἐκκλησίαις. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἄριστα ἔφης. {ΚΥΡ.} Ὅτι τοι προκατηῤῥώστησε μὲν ἡ ἀνθρώπου φύσις τὸν μολυσμὸν, διασμήχοιτο δ' ἂν οὐχ ἑτέρως, πλὴν ὅτι διὰ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κατ' ἀλήθειαν ἱεροῦ καὶ ἁγίου θύματος, εἴσῃ τοι, καὶ μάλα σαφῶς, καὶ ἕτερον ἐπὶ τῷδε τῷ νόμῳ χρησμῴδημα πολυπραγμονῶν. Γέγραπται γὰρ πάλιν ἐν τῷ Λευϊτικῷ· «Καὶ ἐλάλησε Κύριος πρὸς Μωσῆν, λέγων· Λάλησον τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ ἐρεῖς πρὸς αὐτούς· Γυνὴ ἐάν τις σπερματισθῇ, καὶ τέκῃ ἄρσεν, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας, κατὰ τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ χωρισμοῦ τῆς ἀφέδρου αὐτῆς, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται· καὶ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ὀγδόῃ
pass_a_gloss: […] 'you have become a transgressor (parabatēs) of law' (Jas 2:11). For to one who has offended (peplēmmelēkoti) once, that is, because he has transgressed (paranenomēken) at all, even in one and in part, there will follow the need to be charged (enkaleisthai). Polluted (miaros) then by the law, even if one does not go to the extreme of defilement (molysmos), but is caught (kataphōrōito) having suffered it even in part. Yet not entirely cast off (apoblētos); he too is cleansed through water in Christ. So 'unclean until evening' would hint at the time of the sojourn (epidēmia). For at the consummation (synteleia), the age (aiōn) having all but come to its very settings (dysmai), Christ arrived, through whom and in whom we washed off (eknenimmetha) all filth (rhypos) from sin and were freed from small and great charges (aitiamata), we who were held (enischēmenoi) by offences (plēmmeleiai). That before the time of the sojourn it was not possible to wash off defilement (for no one was justified (edikaiouto) in law according to the Scriptures), learn from its saying 'He will be unclean until evening.' PALL.: I understand; the word is true. CYR.: The law adds the matters of a woman flowing (rheousēs) with blood, needing to be defiled, being ill in herself with unchecked (aschetos) downflow (kataphora); and as with the gonorrhyēs every vessel (skeuos), bed (koitē), garment and everyone touching or coming near was defiled, so with her. It frees (apallattei) her the same way: washing with water, turtledoves sacrificed, and the propitiation (hilasmos) of the mediating (mesiteuontos) priest. Bringing us back (anakomizōn) to spiritual thoughts (ennoiai pneumatikai) and not letting us linger (emphilochōrein) in the sicknesses of the flesh (for it was taken as a type (typos) of inward, intelligible (noēta) things), it adds clearly: 'you will make the sons of Israel cautious (eulabeis) from their uncleannesses, and they will not die through their uncleanness, in their defiling my tent (skēnē) among them' (Lev 15:31). Cleansed and sanctified through Christ, then, then we approach bright (lamproi) truly and will no longer defile the holy tent; we will worship (proskynēsomen) pure, purely, the all-holy God, going (phoitōntes) into churches (ekklēsiai). PALL.: Excellently. CYR.: That human nature first fell sick with (prokatērrōstēse) defilement and could be scoured clean no otherwise than through Christ, the truly sacred and holy victim (thyma), you will know if you busy yourself (polypragmonōn) with another oracle (chrēsmōidēma) besides (epi) this law. In Leviticus: 'The Lord spoke to Moses: Speak to the sons of Israel: A woman, if she conceives seed (spermatisthēi) and bears a male, will be unclean seven days; according to the days of the separation (chōrismos) of her menstruation (aphedros) she will be unclean; and on the eighth day […]' (Lev 12:1–3).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …you have become a transgressor of the law’ (James 2:10–11). For whoever has offended once, that is, has broken the law at all, even if only in one point and in part, will surely be liable to the charge. So under the law a person is defiled even if he does not go to the extreme of defilement, but is caught having suffered it even in part. Yet he is not cast off entirely; he too is cleansed through water in Christ. Thus the saying that the defiled man is unclean until evening would point very well to the time of Christ’s coming. For Christ came at the end (Hebrews 9:26), when this age had all but reached its very setting; through him and in him we have washed off all the filth that comes from sin, and we who were held fast by our offenses have been set free from charges both small and great. That before the time of his coming it was not possible to wash away defilement (for, according to the Scriptures, no one was justified by the law (Galatians 3:11)), you may learn from its plain saying: ‘He shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:16).
Palladius: I understand what you say, and the argument is true.

Cyril: To these things the law adds what concerns a woman who has a flow of blood and who, ill in herself with a flow that cannot be checked, is bound to be defiled (Leviticus 15:19–30). And just as with the man with a discharge every vessel was defiled, and every bed, and every garment, and everyone who came near and touched him, so it is with her also. And the law frees her too in the same way as him: by washing her with water, by the sacrifice of turtledoves, and by the atonement made by the mediating priest. But the law, as though lifting us up to spiritual thoughts and not letting us dwell on the ailments of the flesh (for these were taken up as a type of inward realities grasped by the mind), plainly adds: ‘And you shall make the sons of Israel cautious about their uncleannesses, and they shall not die because of their uncleanness when they defile my tent that is among them’ (Leviticus 15:31). For once we have been cleansed and sanctified through Christ, then, yes then, we draw near truly radiant and shall no longer defile the holy tent; and being pure we shall worship the all-holy God purely as we come to the churches.

Cyril: That human nature was first afflicted with defilement, and could be scoured clean in no other way than through Christ, the truly sacred and holy sacrifice, you will know quite clearly if you also look closely at another oracle besides this law.
